beats.say: Open like a teacher: multiplication tables are not just chanted; they have pictures and patterns behind them. We will look at arrays and doubling. No questions.

lines.say: Three times four. Instead of chanting it, let's see it. Multiplication has a picture, and once you've seen the picture the facts stick much better.

beats.say: An array: equal rows and columns of dots. 3 rows of 4 dots shows 3 x 4 = 12. Write the dots on the board line by line, then the multiplication. No questions.

lines.say: An array is a neat arrangement of dots in equal rows. Here's the first row, four dots.
The second row, four dots again.
And a third row. Three rows with four dots in each.
Three rows of four. That's three times four, and if you count the dots, there are twelve.

beats.say: Turn the array: 4 rows of 3 is the same dots, so 4 x 3 = 12. Multiplication can be swapped. Patterns of multiples: 2s even, 5s end in 0 or 5, 10s end in 0. No questions.

lines.say: Now imagine turning our array on its side.
Now we have four rows with three dots in each. Four times three. The same dots, so the same twelve.
Some patterns to spot. Multiples of two are always even.
Multiples of five end in five or zero.
And multiples of ten always end in zero.

beats.say: A friend says 4 x 6 and 6 x 4 give different answers. Test with arrays: 4 rows of 6 = 24; turned, 6 rows of 4 = 24. No questions.

lines.say: A friend of mine thinks four times six and six times four are different, because the numbers are the other way round. Let's test with arrays.
Four rows of six dots. Count them: twenty-four.
Turn it on its side. Now six rows of four. Still twenty-four dots. Nothing was added or lost.
Same array, same total. So the order of a multiplication doesn't matter.

beats.say: Doubling to build tables: 2 x 7 = 14, double it for 4 x 7 = 28, double again for 8 x 7 = 56. No questions.

lines.say: We'll build three facts from each other, starting with the smallest.
A neat trick to build harder tables from easier ones. Start with the two times table. Two sevens are fourteen.
Double the two times table to get the four times table. Four sevens are double fourteen, which is twenty-eight.
Double the four times table to get the eight times table. Eight sevens are double twenty-eight, fifty-six.

beats.say: State the doubling chain as a rule, and the array rule. No questions.

lines.text: Double the 2s  →  the 4s.  Double the 4s  →  the 8s.
lines.say: So: double the twos and you get the fours. Double the fours and you get the eights.

lines.text: An array shows a × b, and turned it shows b × a
lines.say: And whenever you're stuck, draw the array. It shows the multiplication, and turned round it shows the swap too.

beats.say: Do one TOGETHER: 4 x 9 by doubling twice. Questions written on the board first.

lines.say: Now you help me. Four times nine, using doubling. Four is double two.
Start with the easy one.
Now double that.

beats.say: The child works alone: 8 x 6 from 2 x 6 = 12 (double, double); then the array for 3 x 5. Hints only if stuck.

lines.say: Your turn to lead. Eight times six. Start from two sixes, twelve, and double your way up.
First double.
Second double.
Last one, with an array. Three times five.

lines.text: 3 rows of 5 = 15 dots;  turned: 5 rows of 3 = 15 dots
lines.say: The array for three times five is three rows of five, and turned round it is five rows of three, fifteen both ways.

ask.prompt: Describe the array for 3 × 5. What other multiplication does it show when you turn it?
ask.lookFor: 3 rows of 5 gives 15 dots; turned it shows 5 × 3 = 15.
ask.onMiss: Ask: how many rows and how many dots in each? Now turn it on its side.
